newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish court gives green light for Telekom sale.
newsitem.headline: Turkish court gives green light for Telekom sale.

text.p: Turkey's constitutional court on Thursday gave the green light for the sale of Turk Telekom, the centrepiece of the government's privatisation plans, a court official said.
The Istanbul stock market reacted positively to the news, with the main index jumping 4.2 percent in early afternoon trading.
The constitutional court rejected most of a challenge by 116 opposition MPs to the sell-off. "This decision will not block the sale of Telekom shares," a court official said.
The Islamist-led government hopes to raise $3.5 billion from the telecommunications sale, which has been halted three times by the constitutional court since 1993.

The first tranche of up to 15 percent of Telekom is expected to be sold by the end of the year, privatisation officials say. A consortium headed by Goldman Sachs was last month appointed to advise on the sell-off.
Turkey's privatisation programme has moved sluggishly since its inception 10 years ago, raising total revenues of just $3 billion despite bold government forecasts each year.

But State Minister Ufuk Soylemez last week fuelled fresh expectations of accelerated sales, announcing Turkey would prepare at least $750-800 million worth of sell-offs during January, after only $300 million in the whole of 1996.

Recent sales of a bank and tyre and cement factories and the leasing of port facilities have boosted the government's hopes of reaching a target of $5 billion from sell-offs this year. That figure does not include any revenues from Telekom.
Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has dropped previous opposition to privatisation since he formed a coalition with free-marketeer Tansu Ciller last June.
The government is planning to open tenders in the first quarter for the partial sale of state refiner Tupras and petroleum products distributor Petrol Ofisi.

Erbakan said last week the 1996 budget deficit would be 1,200 trillion lira ($10.6 billion), compared with 316.6 trillion a year earlier. Parliament last month approved for 1997 a zero-deficit budget which is based on expectations of considerable revenues from privatisations. ($=114,900 lira)
